event_overview.subject: FAA Resumes Flights After Nationwide Ground Stop Due to System Overload
event_overview.summary: On November 13, 2026, the Federal Aviation Administration imposed a nationwide ground stop for U.S. airports after communications problems affected multiple air-route traffic-control centers. The restriction was a precaution taken amid intermittent telecommunications outages that impaired the stability of air-traffic-control communications and radar; the FAA subsequently cancelled the stop and began restoring departures.

facts.label: Date and duration
facts.value: The disruption began on Friday, November 13, 2026. The Department of Transportation said airspace reopened at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time; the FAA Command Center’s cancellation advisory was issued shortly after 01:19 UTC on November 14.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: The FAA applied the ground stop to all U.S. airports, after communication issues affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

facts.label: Stated safety rationale
facts.value: DOT said the FAA acted out of caution because intermittent telecommunications outages were affecting the stability of communications and radar used by air traffic control.

facts.label: Operational cause under investigation
facts.value: Officials said data inconsistencies arose as legacy switches and routers were overloaded; the FAA’s initial statement characterized the information as preliminary and said technicians were investigating.

facts.label: How a national ground stop works
facts.value: FAA procedures require evaluation of less restrictive measures where possible, coordination across affected facilities and system users, and an advisory describing the national restriction; flights subject to a ground stop are held at their departure points.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War refers here to the 2026 armed conflict between the United States and Iran, including U.S. military operations in and against Iran and maritime-security operations around the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has combined direct military action, disputes over commercial navigation through the strait, and U.S. congressional debate over the President’s authority to continue hostilities.

facts.label: Start of U.S. operation
facts.value: U.S. Central Command says it began Operation Epic Fury against Iran on February 28, 2026, at the President’s direction.

facts.label: Geographic focus
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf, has been a central operational area; CENTCOM described it as an international sea passage and a key trade corridor while conducting mine-clearance and shipping-security operations.

facts.label: Stated U.S. military objectives
facts.value: The White House said the February 28 operation was directed at Iran’s ballistic-missile and drone capabilities, navy, and defense-industrial base; these are stated U.S. objectives, not an independent assessment of the conflict’s effects.

event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War refers here to the 2026 armed conflict between the United States and Iran, including U.S. military operations in and against Iran and maritime-security operations around the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has combined direct military action, disputes over commercial navigation through the strait, and U.S. congressional debate over the President’s authority to continue hostilities.

facts.label: Start of U.S. operation
facts.value: U.S. Central Command says it began Operation Epic Fury against Iran on February 28, 2026, at the President’s direction.

facts.label: Geographic focus
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf, has been a central operational area; CENTCOM described it as an international sea passage and a key trade corridor while conducting mine-clearance and shipping-security operations.

facts.label: Stated U.S. military objectives
facts.value: The White House said the February 28 operation was directed at Iran’s ballistic-missile and drone capabilities, navy, and defense-industrial base; these are stated U.S. objectives, not an independent assessment of the conflict’s effects.

facts.label: Maritime escalation
facts.value: CENTCOM said U.S. strikes beginning July 7 followed attacks on neutral-flagged commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz on July 6–7, with targets including missile sites, air defenses, maritime assets, support infrastructure, and command-and-control capabilities.

facts.label: U.S. war-powers framework
facts.value: Under the War Powers Resolution, the President generally must terminate a reported use of U.S. armed forces within 60 days unless Congress declares war, specifically authorizes the use, extends the period by law, or cannot meet because of an armed attack; the statute also describes removal when Congress directs it by concurrent resolution.

event_overview.title: About Nvidia Scandal
event_overview.subject: Nvidia Scandal
event_overview.summary: “Nvidia scandal” is an informal label for a November 2026 corporate-governance and U.S. national-security controversy involving Nvidia, allegations concerning former chief executive Jensen Huang, and scrutiny of U.S. approvals for advanced AI-chip exports to China-linked buyers. It is not the name of a single formal court case or government proceeding: Nvidia’s public filing confirms Huang’s resignation and leadership transition, while lawmakers and administration officials have raised separate questions about export-control oversight and alleged diversion risks.

facts.label: Corporate transition
facts.value: Nvidia’s board accepted Jen-Hsun (Jensen) Huang’s resignation as president, chief executive officer and board member effective November 11, 2026; it appointed CFO Colette M. Kress interim CEO while it searches for a permanent successor.

facts.label: Company and location
facts.value: Nvidia is a Nasdaq-listed U.S. company; its November 12, 2026 leadership announcement was issued from Santa Clara, California.

facts.label: Export-control authority
facts.value: The U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) administers the relevant semiconductor-export licensing policy. On January 13, 2026, BIS said applications to export Nvidia H200 chips and similar products to China would be reviewed case by case when specified security conditions are met.

facts.label: Congressional scrutiny
facts.value: On November 12, 2026, the ranking members of the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees requested preservation of Commerce Department records concerning Nvidia export-license applications and communications involving Nvidia and Huang. The letter describes allegations and requests records; it is not a finding of wrongdoing.

facts.label: Policy issue at stake
facts.value: The controversy centers on whether controls and due diligence were adequate to prevent advanced U.S. AI chips from reaching unauthorized Chinese end users or being diverted through intermediaries, rather than on a settled legal determination about the allegations involving Huang or any customer.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows major November 13-14, 2026 developments in the political and corporate fallout, but does not by itself establish the truth of espionage-related allegations, resolve any export-control inquiry, or cover every subsequent investigation or legal claim.
